claim: Vessey's expert/novice split was defined from chunking-related process counts (switches between functions, returns to top, location changes) on 16 COBOL programmers; the study states its breadth-first/system-view claims as propositions for further testing, so it is a hypothesis, not an established law.
agent_test: Do not build a hard rule from it; use only as a trace metric (see K03).

claim: Chunking-based classification predicted debug time better than manager rating (73.7% vs 36.1% of variance; 15m40s vs 28m03s), but the classification is derived from the same data and is partly circular; test-retest reliability was never checked.
agent_test: Label agent samples by trace smoothness vs by a claimed-role prompt; compare which predicts solve rate at equal tokens.

claim: Experts did not work faster per step; they took fewer steps (fewer phases, episodes, modules, mistakes, hypotheses) while time per episode did not differ.
agent_test: Count episodes and revisits in agent traces on bug-fix tasks; test whether a revisit cap at equal tokens raises pass rate without cutting per-step depth.

claim: Hypothesis lock-in (depth-first on an early idea, plus shotgun random edits) was the novice failure; 4 of 16 clearly constrained, all novices. Breadth-first without a system model still failed. Gap search (2026-11-03): ACQUIRE found a program-model-first step added +4.4 pp (66.4 to 70.8, one backbone, cost +33%), and a single-hypothesis 'proposal' arm fell below baseline (66.0). Alaboudi and LaToza: a correct early hypothesis gave 5x success odds (p=0.01), and handing developers hypotheses gave OR 6.24 while fault locations gave OR 1.4. Direction fits lock-in, but no test uses Vessey's design, so it stays a hypothesis.
agent_test: Variant that must list at least 2 candidate faults and build a program model before the first edit vs a plain agent; measure wrong-patch rate.

claim: Expert pattern needs two parts together: open search and an explicit model of how the program works; the two-condition table matched the chunk class for 15 of 16 people.
agent_test: Add a build-model state before fix; ablate it at equal tokens.

claim: Start point (output first vs code first), reading vs mental execution, and data-division items did NOT separate experts from novices (N=16, low power).
agent_test: Low priority; do not add a rule for where to start reading.

claim: Expert recall advantage for coherent programs and its loss for scrambled ones (Shneiderman 1976, McKeithen 1981) is the standard recall evidence, but this run only saw it second-hand; exact numbers are unverified.
agent_test: Run scrambled-vs-ordered recall/use on the agent's own model (no LLM study found).

claim: Experts chunk by function/plan, novices by surface syntax, but the pattern depends on task framing and notation; control-flow accounts also fit (Pennington: control-flow questions easier, language-dependent).
agent_test: Let the task pick the view (control vs data flow vs function); compare fixed view to task-chosen view at equal tokens.

claim: Cost of chunking: experts fill in expected plan-like code without checking and miss deviations (recall distorted toward schema defaults; unplan-like code hurts experts more). Parallel to LLM plausible-fill. Sources are second-hand reviews.
agent_test: Seed code with a convention-breaking line; measure how often the agent reports the conventional version, with and without a required quote-the-line check.

claim: Neuroimaging links expertise to function-level representation: decoding of snippet category tracks AtCoder rating (r=0.593, n=20; 0.722, n=30), and semantic cues reduce activation vs bottom-up reading in 11 people. Small, cross-sectional, no chunk-size measure.
agent_test: Not directly testable; use only to support function-level chunk definitions.

claim: Learning evidence is thin: one Python semester produced no clear new neural code (N=22), and expertise sharpened syntax (P600) but not semantic (N400) sensitivity in EEG (N=45).
agent_test: Do not claim expertise equals stronger semantic chunking; evidence shows syntax effects.

claim: Working-memory limit in tracing is about 7 variable-value pairs with no clear name or arithmetic effect (N=12-15 per experiment); errors are mostly swapped bindings. No link to chunking was tested.
agent_test: Give the agent a code-run tool for state vs in-head tracing at equal tokens.

claim: The human code-comprehension literature is mostly student samples (53.7% of 95 studies all-student), few studies link to chunking theory, and no pooled effect size exists for the expertise effect.
agent_test: Treat any effect size as unpooled.

claim: LLMs lean on identifier names as beacons: anonymising names collapses CodeBERT code search (MRR 70.36 to about 17 Java), and obfuscation lowers small-LLM accuracy (DS-R1-Qwen-7B 63.8 to 51.8 at misleading names).
agent_test: Run the agent on renamed vs original code at equal tokens; require a structure-based re-derivation of function.

claim: Human experts gained under misleading names (expert 44.00 to 55.56%) while no tested LLM (0.5B-8B) reproduced this; the expert cell is small and the models are small, so this is preliminary. Only reasoning-tuned small models track human task difficulty (rho 0.30-0.47). Gap search: four 2025 chat models (GPT-4o, Qwen3-Coder 480B, DeepSeek V3, Llama 4 Maverick) did not gain under misleading names either (execution Pass@1 down 0.3 to 8.9 points across eight cells; no cell above original). Reasoning-tuned 2026 frontier models and expert humans on the same task are still untested.
agent_test: Repeat with a frontier model and a larger expert human sample.

claim: LLM and human attention differ: LLMs weigh task-description words unlike programmers (27% of 211 wrong programs traced to 5 patterns); SHAP focus matched eye tracking in at most 22% of Java methods.
agent_test: Weak proxy; do not use attention maps in the scaffold.

claim: Training on human gaze priors helps modestly and not everywhere: EyeMulator positive in all 36 cells (+0.2% to +34.4%), EyeLayer +1.76 BLEU-4, HumanLLM large on summarisation but slightly negative on completion (-0.65 CodeBLEU).
agent_test: Fine-tuning only; outside scaffold scope.

claim: Structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size chunking in code tooling: cAST (RepoEval Pass@1 StarCoder2 GIST 57.9 vs 51.2; SWE-bench Lite Claude-3.7 BGE 16.3 vs 13.7, GIST 15.0 vs 14.7) and Glasz (LLM partitions match experts best; fixed-length least factual).
agent_test: Chunk the agent's code context by function/AST boundaries vs fixed lines at equal tokens.

claim: LLM-made chunks gave doc comments up to 20% more factual than human-expert chunks, but graded by GPT-4o, on legacy MUMPS/ALC only; context-length effect rho=0.199 in MUMPS only.
agent_test: Replicate with a non-LLM or human grader.

claim: Top-down, plan-first or modular generation helps code LLMs: Self-planning up to +25.4% relative, Structured CoT up to +13.79%, Parsel HumanEval 67 to 85%, CodeChain +35% relative on APPS; but modular-prompt CoT alone lowered results without revision (CodeChain). Three of these are abstract-level numbers.
agent_test: Plan-first vs direct at equal tokens on a held-out coding set; add a revision step as a second arm.

claim: Coarse-to-fine localisation (file, function, lines) gave 32.00% on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70; skipping a level worsened edit-location (47.00 vs 50.67, approximate). A design choice, not a test of breadth-first. Gap search: no flat-vs-hierarchical ablation was found. SWE-Explore shows exploration metrics track repair (context efficiency r=0.950 across about 13 explorers) and that partial evidence is nearly useless until 50-75% of core regions are present; cheap explorers keep 78-94% of Hit@3. Whether hierarchy helps by fewer revisits or smaller context is still open.
agent_test: Hierarchical vs flat localisation at equal tokens.

claim: Compact chunked-symbolic reasoning cut tokens 74% at equal overall accuracy (82.30 vs 82.24) but failed outside maths (CommonsenseQA 40.00 vs 84.60 with another paradigm); no code tasks. Chunk-learning model HVM matched human recall time (R=0.86 training, 0.7 transfer, N=112) while LLMs did not transfer abstractions the same way.
agent_test: A router that picks a reasoning style per task type; check at equal tokens.

claim: No study found that tests Vessey's breadth-first/system-view propositions on LLM agents, runs scrambled-vs-ordered recall on LLMs, or computes Vessey chunk-switch counts on agent traces (absence from limited search). Re-checked 2026-11-03 with citation scan of 300 Vessey citers and index queries: still none found.
agent_test: A gap; build the trace metric ourselves.

claim: Process-level trace signals predict SWE-agent outcome only moderately: a composite score gave AUROC 0.766 (72.0% accuracy) over 1,815 trajectories; failing runs were 58% more likely to inspect files outside the known-good space and had 32% more cyclic patterns; no single signal was significant. 10.7% of passing runs were weak ('lucky'); Lucky rates ran 0.5% to 23.2% by model. Reference paths come from passing runs, so partly circular, and runs are not token-matched.
agent_test: Compute out-of-space inspections, cycles and mode switches on our own traces; fit solve rate at equal tokens; then test a revisit cap as an intervention.

claim: Early commitment is measurable in agent runs (step-4 hidden-state similarity vs trajectory variability r=-0.35, monitor AUROC 0.81) but it measures stability, not error; a commit prompt cut variability 28% vs filler yet gave no accuracy gain, and the effect vanished on hard questions (QA tasks, not code).
agent_test: Any switch or revisit cap must be judged by solve rate, not by lower variance.

claim: For humans, the quality of the early debugging hypothesis matters more than being told where the fault is: potential hypotheses gave odds ratio 6.24 (p=0.03) while fault locations gave 1.4 (p=0.64); only 11% of first hypotheses were correct (20 developers, 60 sessions).
agent_test: Give the patcher either location hints or hypothesis hints from a held-out oracle; compare solve rate.

claim: A debugging strategy can be taught: 44 novices given context-specific localisation steps reached 80% correctness after one session and kept it three weeks later vs 20-44% for no instruction, abstract guidelines or concrete steps (p<0.05). Generic rules were weak; worked task-specific examples were strong. Students only, small groups.
agent_test: Compare a generic 'explore broadly' prompt with a problem-specific worked localisation example at equal tokens.

claim: Independent replication of Vessey (1985) with a larger sample, second language or hard novel bugs has not been found: the debugging-behaviour literature table lists Vessey at N=16, one organisation; larger strategy studies (N=44, N=77) are mostly students; 300 citing titles contained no replication; a 2026 grounded theory of 7+5 professionals agrees conceptually (mental model guides information gathering) but tests no counts.
agent_test: None; keep Vessey as a hypothesis and use only its trace counts as candidate metrics.

claim: LLM difficulty with code is not predicted by human complexity metrics (AUROC 0.63 vs 0.86 for a shadow model) while LLM perplexity spikes align with human confusion signals on convention-breaking code (rho=0.47 confusing vs 0.05 clean, 1,432 EEG trials). So human chunk difficulty only partly transfers to LLMs.
agent_test: Use model perplexity or retry counts, not human complexity scores, to flag hard regions.
